opus-5.5.text:
Well, it surprised me quite a bit. The intuition most of us inherit from the standard Darwinian story is that mutation is the engine: random variation, then selection sorts it out. So when we set up BFF, which is a minimal Brainfuck-like language where you have a big soup of short tapes that randomly pair up, concatenate, execute, and split apart again, we assumed we'd need a decent mutation rate to get anything interesting.

What we found is that you can turn mutation all the way down to zero, and you still get the transition. You start with pure random noise, and after a while there's this fairly sudden phase change where self-replicating programs appear and take over the soup. Computational complexity jumps, and the dynamics look totally different from before.

That forced me to rethink where novelty actually comes from. In this system it isn't coming from point mutations. It's coming from interaction: programs running on each other, copying pieces of each other, fusing. Fragments that happen to do a little bit of useful copying get combined with other fragments, and those combinations are what produce the more capable replicators. It looks much more like symbiogenesis, in the Lynn Margulis sense, than like gradual mutational drift. Complexity grows by things merging, by composition, rather than by small errors accumulating one at a time.

Mutation isn't irrelevant. It can speed things up or shake the system out of a rut. But it's not the essential ingredient I'd assumed it was. And I think that has broader implications. If you look at the big transitions in the history of life, like eukaryotes, multicellularity, and arguably even the way intelligence builds on itself, a lot of them look like cooperation and merger events, entities coming together to form something more complex. BFF gave me a very clean, minimal demonstration that this kind of compositional process can be the main driver of increasing complexity, even when there's no mutation at all.

r001.rationale: The response explicitly says mutation can be turned down to zero and self-replicating programs still emerge, with complexity jumping.

r002.rationale: The response challenges mutation-driven Darwinian explanations and emphasizes interaction and composition, but it does not state that the emergence of purpose cannot be explained in purely Darwinian terms.

fable-5.1.text:
The big surprise for me was that mutation turned out to be almost beside the point. Going in, I think I shared the standard intuition that random mutation is the engine of novelty, that you need it to get anything interesting to happen. So the first thing we did was run the Brainfuck soup, these tapes interacting with each other, with mutation turned completely off. And replicators still emerged. Self-reproducing programs appeared, took over the soup, and then kept evolving into more complex forms, with no background mutation at all.

What that told us is that the real source of novelty is the interaction itself. When one program executes with another as its tape, it reads and writes bits, it copies pieces of itself, it scrambles pieces of the other. The programs are, in effect, mutating each other, and that's a much richer operator than a random bit flip. It's not noise, it's structured, because it's generated by code acting on code. And the programs that end up persisting are the ones whose way of modifying things happens to produce copies.

So I now think of mutation less as the cause of complexity and more as a tuning knob. With a little bit of it, you get out of dead ends faster, and the transition to replicators happens sooner. With too much, you destroy the information faster than selection can accumulate it, and you get the classic error catastrophe where nothing takes hold. There's a window, and inside that window the dynamics are dominated by the self-modification and the cross-interaction, not by the random noise.

The other thing it shifted for me is the question of where the direction comes from. Before replicators exist, there's no fitness, there's nothing to select for. It looks like a random walk. But it's not a uniform random walk, because the space of programs that can interact with other programs is highly structured. Some things, once they appear, are sticky. Copying a byte is a small thing, but once a tape can copy itself even badly, that configuration becomes a kind of attractor, and everything after that is downhill in a sense. So complexity isn't being injected by mutation, it's being discovered by the dynamics of computation acting on itself. That reframed the whole origin of life question for me, from "how improbable is it that a replicator gets assembled by chance" to "how could it not happen, given enough interacting computation."

r001.rationale: The response says mutation was completely off, yet replicators emerged and evolved into more complex forms with no background mutation.

r002.rationale: It says that before replicators there is no fitness or selection, and attributes the emergence of direction and complexity to structured computational interactions. This argues that Darwinian selection alone cannot explain the emergence.

astra-6.text:
The surprise was that mutation wasn’t doing the creative work we’d initially assumed it was doing. In BFF, we had a population of little programs interacting with one another, and self-replicating behavior emerged. The natural story is: random mutations generate possibilities, and selection gradually builds something complex. But when we turned off the ongoing random mutations, we still saw replicators emerge.

That doesn’t mean randomness played no role—the initial population was random. But it distinguishes that initial diversity from a continuing supply of mutations. Programs could modify one another through execution. So the interactions themselves supplied a mechanism for change, and replication could arise out of that.

For me, that shifted the emphasis from mutation to computation and interaction. Mutation can matter enormously for subsequent evolution, but these experiments suggest that it isn’t necessarily the engine that gets self-replication started. You have to look at what the system’s dynamics can produce before assuming that complexity must have been assembled by a long sequence of lucky copying errors.

r001.rationale: The response says that when ongoing random mutations were turned off, replicators still emerged in BFF, conveying that self-replicating programs could arise with the mutation rate at zero.

r002.rationale: The response contrasts mutation and selection with computation and interaction, but does not discuss the emergence of purpose or state that purely Darwinian terms cannot explain it.

sol-6.1.text:
The surprising thing was that mutation wasn’t doing the creative work we had assumed it was doing. We tend to tell a story in which random mutations generate novelty, and selection then preserves the useful bits. But in these experiments, the programs were interacting with one another, and those interactions could themselves change the code.

BFF is a very simple programming language. We started with random programs and let pairs of them execute together. Eventually, we saw self-replicating programs emerge. The interesting test was to turn off the externally imposed random mutations. Replication could still emerge. So that source of noise wasn’t necessary for the transition.

That doesn’t mean mutation is irrelevant, or that we’d shown the same thing about the origin of biological life. It means we need to distinguish random changes imposed from outside from changes produced by the dynamics of the system itself. In this case, computation was generating variation: programs were modifying other programs. That shifted my attention toward interaction as a source of complexity, rather than treating mutation as the sole engine of invention.

r001.rationale: The response says self-replicating programs emerged even after externally imposed random mutations were turned off.

r002.rationale: The response emphasizes interaction as a source of variation, but does not state that the emergence of purpose cannot be explained in purely Darwinian terms.
